bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Commodity price volatility in agricultural raw materials — The business is vulnerable to fluctuations in the availability and price of agricultural commodities; inability to secure high-quality ingredients at predictable costs may compress margins. FY'26 saw prolonged deflation in spices (particularly chilli) that held revenue growth to 3.0% despite 6.4% volume growth, followed by a sharp price increase towards the fourth quarter. Mitigation rests on a manufacturing footprint located near key demand and sourcing centres, strategic inventory and opportunity buying on market intelligence, a diversified supplier base, and brand equity strong enough to make price increases stick.
- Geopolitical uncertainty and supply chain disruption — An unstable geopolitical environment disrupts supply chains, raises input and logistics costs and introduces trade-policy uncertainty, affecting sourcing, production and distribution efficiency and potentially compressing margins. The West Asia conflict caused elevated freight costs, port disruptions and extended transit timelines during FY'26, while tariff actions in the United States hurt the North America business. Mitigated through continuous evaluation of market volatility, buffer stock policies and a diversified vendor base.
- Macroeconomic slowdown and shifts in consumer spending — Inflation and changes in consumer spending patterns directly affect the business; a slowdown in the Indian economy could reduce discretionary spending on packaged food. Mitigated through volume-led growth focused on preserving and expanding household reach, a portfolio architecture spanning affordable to premium, expanding digital commerce presence and disciplined cost management.
- Intense competition in a fragmented packaged food industry — The Company faces pressure from large multinationals as well as local organised and unorganised players, which may influence market share and pricing power. Defence rests on decades-old brand leadership in core markets, regional taste specificity, commercially validated innovation, deep core-market distribution plus rapidly expanding digital commerce, and localised brand-building.
- Changing consumer preferences and category shifts — Inability to anticipate and respond in a timely manner to evolving consumer preferences and market shifts in key categories may lead to weaker growth and erosion of market position. Managed through continuous innovation, portfolio diversification into adjacent high-growth segments (ready-to-eat sweets, convenience formats, global cuisine-inspired ranges), third-party data analytics, market research and pilot sampling before full-scale launches.
- Food safety and quality compliance — Inadequate adherence to product quality standards and local and global food regulations threatens operations and reputation; even isolated quality lapses may erode consumer trust, while non-compliance can bring regulatory action, penalties and suspension of business activities. Managed through a multi-layered quality governance framework covering owned and third-party plants, strict adherence to GMP, GHP and Food Safety and Standards Regulations, supplier qualification and monitoring, contract-manufacturer audits held to the same standards, and a dedicated regulatory affairs team.
- Cyber security — Cyberattacks arising from infrastructure vulnerabilities, inadequate protocols or human error could compromise sensitive information and disrupt operations, exposing the Company to financial loss, regulatory action, litigation and reputational damage. Mitigated via regular VAPT, continuous endpoint and perimeter threat monitoring, role-based access, segregation-of-duties reviews, multi-factor authentication, privileged access monitoring, endpoint detection and response, automated patch management and employee training.
- People, talent continuity and business ethics/compliance — Loss of critical talent, gaps in succession planning and lapses in occupational health and safety can impair organisational capability and leadership continuity, while breaches of statutory, regulatory or ethical standards expose the Company to penalties, scrutiny and reputational damage. Permanent-employee attrition ran at 23% in FY'26 (versus 20% in FY'25). Managed through defined succession planning for critical roles, regular talent reviews and internal development, alongside an Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption policy with mandatory training, Code of Conduct adherence from hiring, an automated compliance monitoring tool and third-party due diligence.
- Concentration in South India, in the spices category and in a distributor-led B2B route to market — Structural concentration disclosed rather than labelled as risk: grinding and processing of spices contributes 70.2% of turnover, core market strength is concentrated in Karnataka, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, exports contribute 21% of turnover (with the GCC dominant within international), and products are sold primarily under a B2B model exclusively to distributors, with a direct network only in Kerala.
- Climate change — Identified as a material ESG risk in the Double Materiality Assessment: increasing frequency of extreme weather events and evolving climatic conditions may affect the availability of key raw materials and disrupt the supply chain, while tightening emissions and energy-efficiency regulation may raise compliance and transition costs. Mitigation is GHG emissions reduction via an increased share of renewable energy and investment in low-carbon technologies, with short-term negative capital expenditure implications and long-term positive efficiency benefits.

outlook.body:
- Build depth over breadth: pursue regional relevance in the cuisines and communities where MTR and Eastern belong rather than chasing national scale at the cost of local relevance
- Anchor growth in 'convenience meets authenticity' - the intersection management identifies as its greatest long-term opportunity as households shrink, women's workforce participation rises and millennials/Gen Z demand speed without losing regional authenticity
- Drive consumer-led growth through rigorous brand building, purposeful innovation and deep market understanding, backed by an innovation engine of 37 product development specialists, seven chefs and a repository of over 4,000 recipes
- Project Bolt - a focused initiative to accelerate digital commerce growth via a dedicated execution playbook, winning online market share and digital-first innovations aligned to platform-specific consumer needs, supported by organisation design, team capability, consumer insights and technology-driven decision-making
- Restructure Eastern's distribution network in Kerala to build a more efficient, scalable and future-ready route-to-market as general trade evolves through consolidation and competition from modern and digital channels
- Accelerate AI adoption across the organisation - embedding actionable insights into work processes, providing AI-generated insights to managers, automating tasks through Agentic AI and engaging digital-native consumers
- Strengthen the manufacturing footprint through a balanced mix of large-scale facilities and agile, distributed units to respond to evolving business needs and build a more efficient supply chain
- Expand household penetration and consumption occasions in spices through deeper market penetration, targeted consumer activations and culturally rooted regional communication
- Premiumise and go digital-first in spices via MTR Prakriti, a single-origin offering with a dedicated direct-to-consumer platform targeting an all-India, metropolitan consumer base
- Expand convenience foods reach across India, particularly the top 28 metropolitan markets, through innovation, distribution expansion and consumer-centric offerings
- Deepen the international franchise among the Indian diaspora and extend to the Arab consumer base in the GCC through smaller pack sizes for traditional trade, refreshed packaging and targeted digital campaigns
- Maintain operational resilience through proactive risk management, diversified sourcing strategies, strong supply chain planning, disciplined cost management and productivity improvement initiatives
- Strengthen governance post-listing - a full and balanced Board with new independent directors, new leadership talent, and greater transparency and accountability as a listed company
- The routed text states no dividend quantum, payout ratio or reinvestment philosophy. It confirms only that a Dividend Distribution Policy is one of the Company's formally adopted corporate policies, alongside a Risk Management Policy, Whistleblower Policy, Nomination and Remuneration Policy, Succession Planning Policy, Policy for determining Material Subsidiary, Policy on Materiality of Related Party Transactions and an Environmental, Social & Governance Policy. Governance intent is framed as laying the foundation for long-term value creation for shareholders, employees and society at large, with the Board providing strategic oversight and ensuring fiscal discipline. On employee capital, the 30th AGM (August 19, 2026) seeks ratification of the Employee Stock Option Plan 2025, approved by the Board on May 12, 2025 and by shareholders on May 16, 2025 prior to the IPO listing. There are no shares in the demat/unclaimed suspense account and no agreements requiring disclosure under clause 5A of Schedule III of the SEBI Listing Regulations.
- Conducted a Double Materiality Assessment in 2024 - evaluating both the actual and potential impacts of operations on environment and society and the financial risks and opportunities arising from ESG factors over short, medium and long term - using desktop research, stakeholder identification and engagement, internal workshops and management inputs, with employees, suppliers, customers and regulators consulted
- Material ESG topics identified and forming the basis of BRSR disclosure - Environmental: Climate Change, Resource Use and Circular Economy; Social: Health and Nutrition, Occupational Health and Safety, Responsible Sourcing, Training and Skill Development, Safe Products; Governance: Business Conduct
- Climate commitment: reduce GHG emissions by increasing the share of renewable energy and investing in low-carbon technologies, accepting short-term capital expenditure for long-term emissions reduction and energy efficiency gains (no quantified target or target year disclosed)
- Responsible sourcing treated as both risk and opportunity - promoting sustainable agricultural practices to enable farmers to adopt climate-resilient practices, prioritising fair treatment and payment for suppliers to support livelihoods, mitigate labour-dispute risk and reinforce transparency
- Quality and safe products governance extends to third parties: all owned and contract manufacturing units adhere to Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP), Good Hygiene Practices (GHP) and Food Safety and Standards Regulations (FSSR), with periodic independent audits, structured supplier qualification and contractual quality obligations for contract manufacturers
- Business conduct framework anchored by a formal Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption policy with mandatory employee training, annual refreshers, Code of Conduct adherence from hiring, an automated regulatory compliance monitoring tool mapping requirements to responsible employees, and third-party due diligence in supplier onboarding
- Diversity: women represent 37.5% of the Board of Directors and 33.3% of Key Management Personnel; women are 22% of total employees and 47% of total workers
- Attrition disclosed on a three-year trend - permanent employees 23% in FY 2025-26 versus 20% in FY 2024-25 and 31% in FY 2023-24; permanent workers 12% versus 15% and 10%
- Grievance redressal mechanisms are in place for all stakeholder groups (communities, investors, shareholders, employees and workers, customers, value chain partners); in FY 2025-26 four whistleblower complaints were received from employees and workers and all were resolved, and 282 customer complaints were received of which one remained pending
- No independent assurance of the BRSR was undertaken for the reporting year; the Company states the disclosures were prepared in alignment with its internal data governance and quality control processes, on a standalone reporting boundary
- Risk Management Committee meets periodically to provide oversight and strategic guidance on implementation and monitoring of mitigation actions, with business risks and opportunities systematically identified, assessed and managed on an ongoing basis

outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: The annual report does not disclose a named capex programme, project cost, commissioning schedule or installed-capacity addition. Expansion is described as footprint- and distribution-led rather than plant-led. The company operates eight manufacturing units - Bommasandra, Hennagra, Tumkur, Kothamangalam, Adimali Unit I, Adimali Unit II, Guntur and Ramganjmandi - supplemented by a contract manufacturing network of 17 domestic and 3 overseas units, a head office in Bengaluru with additional offices in Kochi, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Delhi, Chennai and Mumbai, and an international office in Dubai under Orkla IMEA Trading, a 100% subsidiary. Growth capacity is being added through channel and market reach: an expanding distribution network across general trade, modern trade, digital commerce and export channels, a strategic focus on expanding convenience-foods reach across India and particularly the top 28 metropolitan markets, and an international footprint spanning 45 countries with strong positions in the GCC, USA, Canada, UK, Australia and New Zealand. In spices, the company launched MTR Prakriti, a premium single-origin digital-first brand supported by a dedicated direct-to-consumer platform and a digital-commerce-led model that extends consumer access beyond traditional distribution channels. In the GCC the Eastern Arabic range was newly established with smaller pack sizes suited to traditional trade, refreshed packaging and targeted digital campaigns. Management also notes that in the convenience foods portfolio the fresh batter business is progressively scaling up and is expected to contribute meaningfully to future growth, and that the Meals platform will see continued focus on portfolio expansion. Sector-level capacity policy support is cited (PLI Scheme for Food Processing incentivising incremental sales and capacity creation, PMFME, PMKSY infrastructure investments and 100% FDI under the automatic route) but no company-specific participation or investment is stated.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Structural tailwinds in the Indian food market: a large and increasingly aspirational population, growing disposable incomes and a sustained shift toward quality packaged foods
- Only about 32% of total food is processed in India today, leaving immense untapped potential; rising per capita incomes drive a clear consumer shift from unbranded to branded, while urbanisation pushes demand from basic to higher value-added processing
- India's packaged food industry, estimated at approximately INR 10,180 billion in FY'24, is expected to grow at a CAGR of ~11% to reach INR 17,120 billion by FY'29
- The Indian packaged spices market, approximately INR 345 billion in FY'24, is projected to reach around INR 615 billion by FY'29; blended spices are growing faster than pure spices on rising adoption of ready-to-use, dish-specific mixes
- South India accounts for ~35% of the domestic packaged spices market (~INR 121 billion in FY'24) and is expected to grow at a CAGR of ~11.7% to ~INR 210 billion by FY'29 - the company's heartland and a strong base for distribution-led growth and brand-led consolidation
- India's convenience food market, valued at approximately INR 79 billion in FY'24, is projected to reach around INR 166 billion by FY'29 at a CAGR of approximately 16%, driven by nuclear households, higher disposable incomes, greater female workforce participation and fading culinary skills among millennials and Gen Z
- Spices export market valued at approximately INR 370 billion in FY'24 is expected to grow at a CAGR of ~13.8% to ~INR 705 billion by FY'29, supported by global demand for authentic Indian flavours and expansion of the Indian diaspora; branded packaged spices are gaining traction versus bulk exports
- Channel shift: general trade remains dominant while modern trade and digital commerce grow rapidly, including the remarkable rise of quick commerce, improving accessibility and accelerating category adoption
- Premiumisation, health-conscious consumption and clean-label preferences are shaping product development across the industry
- Emerging consumer archetypes - the conscious eater, curious indulger, comfort and heritage seeker and value convenience seeker - are creating significant headroom for packaged food, making innovation a key driver of growth
- Policy support: PLI Scheme for Food Processing (~INR 109 billion outlay), PMFME (INR 100 billion), PMKSY (over INR 60 billion phased), GST rate reductions from 12% and 18% to 5% on packaged and convenience foods improving affordability, and 100% FDI under the automatic route
- India's macro backdrop: real GDP growth estimated at 7.7% in FY'26 with the RBI projecting around 6.6% for FY'27, a 100 bps repo rate cut during the year, and domestic demand expected to remain the primary growth driver with private consumption staying healthy
- Global economy expected to grow around 3.1% in CY'26 and 3.2% in CY'27, reflecting subdued expansion across major economies
- Spices deflation, particularly in chilli over the last two years, tempered value growth while volumes grew; spice prices rose significantly towards the end of FY'26, prompting calibrated price increases
- New product launches contributed 3.6% of FY'26 revenues, with convenience foods delivering strong double-digit growth

Mitigated via regular VAPT, continuous endpoint and perimeter threat monitoring, role-based access, segregation-of-duties reviews, multi-factor authentication, privileged access monitoring, endpoint detection and response, automated patch management and employee training.

risks.note: Loss of critical talent, gaps in succession planning and lapses in occupational health and safety can impair organisational capability and leadership continuity, while breaches of statutory, regulatory or ethical standards expose the Company to penalties, scrutiny and reputational damage. Permanent-employee attrition ran at 23% in FY'26 (versus 20% in FY'25). Managed through defined succession planning for critical roles, regular talent reviews and internal development, alongside an Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption policy with mandatory training, Code of Conduct adherence from hiring, an automated compliance monitoring tool and third-party due diligence.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Orkla India Limited is a leading multi-category Indian food company built on heritage brands MTR, Eastern and Rasoi Magic, holding the No. 1 position in packaged spices in Karnataka and Kerala while serving the Indian diaspora across 45 countries.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Orkla India manufactures, markets and sells packaged food products in India and international markets, operating across pure spices, blended spices and convenience foods such as ready-to-cook and ready-to-eat meals, breakfast mixes, fresh batters, vermicelli and sweets. Its portfolio is anchored by MTR and Eastern, with deep roots in Karnataka, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana and a pan-India presence across major metro cities. The company operates primarily on a business-to-business model selling to distributors who supply retailers and e-commerce channels, with a direct distribution network in Kerala and direct warehouse-to-seller supply for large modern trade, quick commerce and e-commerce partners.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Structural tailwinds in the Indian food market: a large and increasingly aspirational population, growing disposable incomes and a sustained shift toward quality packaged foods
- Only about 32% of total food is processed in India today, leaving immense untapped potential; rising per capita incomes drive a clear consumer shift from unbranded to branded, while urbanisation pushes demand from basic to higher value-added processing
- India's packaged food industry, estimated at approximately INR 10,180 billion in FY'24, is expected to grow at a CAGR of ~11% to reach INR 17,120 billion by FY'29
- The Indian packaged spices market, approximately INR 345 billion in FY'24, is projected to reach around INR 615 billion by FY'29; blended spices are growing faster than pure spices on rising adoption of ready-to-use, dish-specific mixes
- South India accounts for ~35% of the domestic packaged spices market (~INR 121 billion in FY'24) and is expected to grow at a CAGR of ~11.7% to ~INR 210 billion by FY'29 - the company's heartland and a strong base for distribution-led growth and brand-led consolidation
- India's convenience food market, valued at approximately INR 79 billion in FY'24, is projected to reach around INR 166 billion by FY'29 at a CAGR of approximately 16%, driven by nuclear households, higher disposable incomes, greater female workforce participation and fading culinary skills among millennials and Gen Z
- Spices export market valued at approximately INR 370 billion in FY'24 is expected to grow at a CAGR of ~13.8% to ~INR 705 billion by FY'29, supported by global demand for authentic Indian flavours and expansion of the Indian diaspora; branded packaged spices are gaining traction versus bulk exports
- Channel shift: general trade remains dominant while modern trade and digital commerce grow rapidly, including the remarkable rise of quick commerce, improving accessibility and accelerating category adoption
- Premiumisation, health-conscious consumption and clean-label preferences are shaping product development across the industry
- Emerging consumer archetypes - the conscious eater, curious indulger, comfort and heritage seeker and value convenience seeker - are creating significant headroom for packaged food, making innovation a key driver of growth
- Policy support: PLI Scheme for Food Processing (~INR 109 billion outlay), PMFME (INR 100 billion), PMKSY (over INR 60 billion phased), GST rate reductions from 12% and 18% to 5% on packaged and convenience foods improving affordability, and 100% FDI under the automatic route
- India's macro backdrop: real GDP growth estimated at 7.7% in FY'26 with the RBI projecting around 6.6% for FY'27, a 100 bps repo rate cut during the year, and domestic demand expected to remain the primary growth driver with private consumption staying healthy
- Global economy expected to grow around 3.1% in CY'26 and 3.2% in CY'27, reflecting subdued expansion across major economies
- Spices deflation, particularly in chilli over the last two years, tempered value growth while volumes grew; spice prices rose significantly towards the end of FY'26, prompting calibrated price increases
- New product launches contributed 3.6% of FY'26 revenues, with convenience foods delivering strong double-digit growth

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: The annual report does not disclose a named capex programme, project cost, commissioning schedule or installed-capacity addition. Expansion is described as footprint- and distribution-led rather than plant-led. The company operates eight manufacturing units - Bommasandra, Hennagra, Tumkur, Kothamangalam, Adimali Unit I, Adimali Unit II, Guntur and Ramganjmandi - supplemented by a contract manufacturing network of 17 domestic and 3 overseas units, a head office in Bengaluru with additional offices in Kochi, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Delhi, Chennai and Mumbai, and an international office in Dubai under Orkla IMEA Trading, a 100% subsidiary. Growth capacity is being added through channel and market reach: an expanding distribution network across general trade, modern trade, digital commerce and export channels, a strategic focus on expanding convenience-foods reach across India and particularly the top 28 metropolitan markets, and an international footprint spanning 45 countries with strong positions in the GCC, USA, Canada, UK, Australia and New Zealand. In spices, the company launched MTR Prakriti, a premium single-origin digital-first brand supported by a dedicated direct-to-consumer platform and a digital-commerce-led model that extends consumer access beyond traditional distribution channels. In the GCC the Eastern Arabic range was newly established with smaller pack sizes suited to traditional trade, refreshed packaging and targeted digital campaigns. Management also notes that in the convenience foods portfolio the fresh batter business is progressively scaling up and is expected to contribute meaningfully to future growth, and that the Meals platform will see continued focus on portfolio expansion. Sector-level capacity policy support is cited (PLI Scheme for Food Processing incentivising incremental sales and capacity creation, PMFME, PMKSY infrastructure investments and 100% FDI under the automatic route) but no company-specific participation or investment is stated.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Heritage brand equity: MTR (100 years of legacy) and Eastern command deep consumer trust in their home markets, with MTR described as part of Karnataka's culinary heritage
- No. 1 position in packaged spices in both Karnataka and Kerala
- Eastern is the No. 1 Indian spice brand in the UAE by household reach, supported by strong distribution and deep diaspora connect
- Largest exporter of branded spices for 24 consecutive years, with a footprint spanning 45 countries
- Extensive distribution reach of around 679,000 retail touchpoints in FY'26 across general trade, modern trade and digital commerce, plus a direct distribution network in Kerala
- Integrated manufacturing and sourcing network of 8 owned units plus 17 domestic and 3 overseas contract manufacturers, backed by longstanding supplier partnerships
- Deep understanding of regional Indian cuisines enabling localised product innovation (region-specific chilli and masala variants, Thaninadan Sambar, 5-Minute Breakfast range)
- Parentage of Orkla ASA, providing global brand-building expertise, stringent compliance standards and centres of excellence in sustainability, marketing and innovation, IT, sales and procurement
- Profitable international portfolio mix led by blended spices and convenience foods with strong market execution capabilities

- Anchor growth in 'convenience meets authenticity' - the intersection management identifies as its greatest long-term opportunity as households shrink, women's workforce participation rises and millennials/Gen Z demand speed without losing regional authenticity
- Drive consumer-led growth through rigorous brand building, purposeful innovation and deep market understanding, backed by an innovation engine of 37 product …

themes.title: Consumption revival & FMCG premiumization
themes.need: Rural recovery, GST 2.0 and premiumization still frame the theme, but Q1FY27 rewarded portfolio SHAPE over volume. TATACONSUM's growth businesses hit INR 1,300cr (+47%) and are now 36% of India - larger than either salt (>INR 1,000cr) or tea & coffee (INR 1,200cr), with Sampann +58%, RTD +41% and Capital Foods INR 232cr (+40%) - while India tea revenue fell 4% on +2% volume as lower tea costs were deliberately passed back (tea inflation is now running 7-10% with most buying still ahead, so that inverts next year). PGHH shows the margin route: FY26 sales roughly flat at ~INR 4,300cr but PAT +19% to ~INR 850cr and ~100bps of structural margin from INR 86cr of productivity savings, absorbing crude and resin each up 30-50% with no stock-outs. The cautionary tale is licensed brands - JYOTHYLAB lost the Pril and Fa licences when Henkel did not renew (all manufacturing and selling stopped 1-June; Pril was ~7-8% of revenue, ~INR 225-240cr) and has filed SIAC arbitration. MARICO/DABUR/GODREJCP/COLPAL/EMAMILTD ride distribution + premium mix; VBL on beverage route-to-market; BIKAJI/GOPAL/BECTORFOOD on branded snacks; ORKLAINDIA took a 4% blended price increase in Q4 plus premium mix to a 16.9% EBITDA margin.
themes.driver: GST 2.0 demand pull-through; rural volume recovery; festive/wedding restocking; commodity pass-back timing; JYOTHYLAB's ~7-8% revenue hole and the SIAC arbitration.
